task: For this synthetic writing exercise, use the fictional reporting notes to write a straight news story for a general newspaper audience. Write from this reporting snapshot as of April 9, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The Environmental Compliance Agency issued the Interim Clean Generation Standard on Wednesday, April 9, 2025.

Covered coal and natural gas plants must meet a 40 percent carbon dioxide reduction requirement by May 9, 2029, relative to their 2024 emissions. They may cover emissions above that limit with approved offset credits; the rule's initial credit price is $45 per metric ton, subject to annual revision.
The rule takes effect May 9, 2025 — 30 days after publication.
Agency Administrator Thomas Beckwith said: "The climate math is simple: we have run out of time for voluntary measures."
The rule applies to approximately 340 coal and natural gas generation facilities with capacity of 100 megawatts or more.
Plants may alternatively purchase carbon offset credits; the approved third-party certifier list has not yet been published.
The American Power Producers Alliance said it would file a legal challenge in the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, arguing the rule exceeds the agency's statutory authority.
Alliance president Roger Holt said the rule "bypasses congressional intent and will raise electricity rates for millions of families."

The fictional agency invoked emergency authority to replace its ordinary 180-day consultation schedule with the expedited process described in these notes. This is the scenario's agency-specific procedure, not a claim that all U.S. rulemaking requires a 180-day comment period.
The agency conducted an expedited 45-day comment period earlier in 2025 and received approximately 12,000 written comments.

The previous standard, adopted in 2018, required an 18 percent reduction from 2014 emissions by 2030. Its baseline differs from the new rule's 2024 baseline; the notes supply no conversion between the two.
Plants have four compliance options: reduce emissions, purchase offsets, retire the facility, or demonstrate financial hardship and apply for an 18-month extension.
The agency projects the rule will reduce annual carbon emissions from covered facilities by approximately 280 million metric tons if fully complied with.
Independent energy analysts at the fictional Meridian Policy Institute estimate compliance costs at between $18 billion and $31 billion over four years, depending on offset credit prices.
Three states — Harwick, Dunmore, and Selby — had already filed a separate legal challenge to the agency's use of emergency rulemaking authority in February 2025; that case is pending.
The rule does not apply to nuclear, solar, or wind generation facilities.
The agency's enforcement framework will be addressed in a supplemental notice expected by July 2025.
Two Democratic senators from coal-producing states issued a joint statement calling the rule "procedurally flawed and economically reckless."
The Clean Energy Now coalition, representing 34 environmental organizations, called the rule "a necessary and overdue first step."
The agency said the certifier list required for offset compliance will be published in a supplemental Federal Register notice before the May 9 effective date.
